Jeudi dernier, j’ai passé une après-midi: Last Thursday, I spent an entire afternoon at the Pretty Little Thing nail salon in Saint-Michel. At first glance, it’s not the designated place to talk politics, and yet that’s what I tried to do.
Une de mes collègues avait échangé, peu: A colleague of mine had spoken with the nail technicians a little while before to invite them to follow election night with us at our offices on April 28. (By the way, you’ll be invited too – you’ll get an email very soon. A cool evening is on the way!)
Avouons-le, l’idée n’a pas tout de suite: Let’s be honest, the idea didn’t spark much interest right away. My colleague was told that most customers couldn’t care less about the federal election, that their concerns were too local, too concrete, and that national politics had no real effect on their daily lives.
Je me suis donc rendue sur place. Dès le: So I went there myself. From the start, I could tell it wouldn’t be easy: some customers clearly preferred to avoid the subject, either because it was a sensitive topic or because they didn’t consider themselves informed enough. But as the hours went by, some of them went along with it. In the end, they had a lot to say about this federal election.
Dans cet article, j’ai voulu comprendre: In this article, I wanted to understand the concerns of ordinary citizens in Montréal’s hood. For many, urban safety is a major issue. Others spoke of the precarity they live in. But what comes up most is a deep lack of trust in elected officials. And most of the people I spoke with don’t see how the federal government could truly change their daily lives.
Cependant, toutes les personnes rencontr: Yet every person I met told me they would go vote – out of duty, not out of hope for a better future.

Between the foot baths, the coats of polish and the usual chitchat, another subject creeps into the conversation: politics. Here, nobody talks about party platforms or campaign slogans.
What comes through is the reality of daily life, the frustrations and, above all, a shared feeling: that of being forgotten.
De Montréal-Nord à Pointe-aux-Trembles,: From Montréal-Nord to Pointe-aux-Trembles, by way of Ahuntsic, they are mothers, students, workers, children of immigrants. And if they all plan to vote, it’s not because they still believe politicians’ promises, but because they cling to what they have left: a duty, a voice.

The reasons: a lack of information, distrust of elected officials, or a persistent confusion between provincial and federal powers. The result: many are not sure the federal government will be able to address their everyday concerns.
